edition.deck: Political fallout in the US, a fresh strike on Iran and new scrutiny of critical infrastructure lead the morning’s coverage.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises overnight developments and consequential current affairs, with fresh Danish reporting. Returning coverage is included only where the gather supplies a meaningful development.

content.headline: Paraguay’s president impeached after bank collapse leaves millions without funds
content.shortHeadline: Paraguay president impeached after bank collapse
content.standfirst: Santiago Peña was removed and placed under house arrest after lawmakers blamed him for alleged conflicts of interest and oversight failures linked to Ueno Bank’s collapse. He denies wrongdoing; millions of depositors remain unable to access savings.

image.caption: Political drama followed Peña’s impeachment and arrest.

sources.originalTitle: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested

segments.body: Paraguay’s Senate voted 44 to one to impeach President Santiago Peña after the collapse of Ueno Bank left an estimated three million people unable to access savings and pensions. He was placed under house arrest and is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations including breach of trust and misappropriation of funds.

segments.title: The allegations and the response
segments.body: The impeachment charges allege conflicts of interest, interference with regulatory oversight and the diversion of pension funds. Peña, who held shares in the bank’s parent company until last year, denies wrongdoing. Vice-President Pedro Alliana has been sworn in as interim president and says affected depositors will be compensated.

content.headline: US says it carried out another limited strike on Iran as talks continue
content.shortHeadline: US reports another limited strike on Iran
content.standfirst: Donald Trump called the action against an Iranian air-defence system “minor”, while Tehran’s state media reported explosions on Qeshm Island. The strikes come amid negotiations to end the war, with no agreement announced.

image.caption: Donald Trump speaks to reporters after announcing another limited strike on Iran.

sources.originalTitle: US carries out another round of ‘minor’ strikes on Iran, Trump says
Trump wants to ‘go after’ Iran’s nuclear mountain. Could the unthinkable happen?

segments.body: Donald Trump said US forces struck an Iranian air-defence system on Friday, describing the action as “minor”. Iranian state media reported two explosions near Suza on Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz. US Central Command had also reported “defensive” strikes earlier in the week.

segments.title: Unresolved risks
segments.body: Trump says talks with Iran are continuing, and diplomatic calls involving Qatar have sought to reduce tensions. The nuclear programme remains a central obstacle. A separate report says some military specialists see a nuclear strike as highly unlikely, while warning that any such use would cross a major threshold; the supplied reporting does not indicate that one is being prepared.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s reporting focuses on the risks around Iran’s deeply buried nuclear site. Specialists it quotes say a conventional attack may not destroy the facility, but several argue that a nuclear strike would be an extraordinary escalation and see no evidence one is imminent.

content.headline: Global markets steady after a sharp sell-off tied to AI fears
content.shortHeadline: Markets rebound partly after AI-led sell-off
content.standfirst: US technology shares recovered some ground on Friday after steep losses spread to Asia and Europe. Investors remain divided over whether AI valuations are due for a lasting correction or whether political concerns about data centres have intensified the turbulence.

image.caption: Traders at the New York Stock Exchange during Thursday’s sell-off.

sources.originalTitle: Global stocks fall amid ‘big worries over AI’ after Democrats’ midterms triumph
US tech stock rout: is the AI bubble bursting?
Why the US midterms sparked an AI stock selloff

segments.body: The Nasdaq fell 5.5% on Thursday, its sharpest one-day drop in 19 months, and the S&P 500 lost 4.4%. Asian markets also fell sharply on Friday. US shares rose when trading resumed, but the rebound recovered only part of the previous day’s losses.

segments.title: What is driving the anxiety?
segments.body: The sell-off has been linked to fears that a Democratic-controlled Congress could restrict AI and data-centre expansion, as well as longer-running doubts about whether huge investments in AI will deliver expected returns. The Guardian reports that more than $3.2tn was wiped from US market value on Thursday.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s analysis stresses that concern about AI valuations predates the election result. It also points to local opposition to data centres over their demands on water, electricity and land as one reason investors are watching the political response.

segments.title: Investors disagree on what comes next
segments.body: Analysts quoted by the Guardian differ over whether the sell-off signals a longer downturn: some warn of further selling, while others say AI investment is still likely to support growth. Most major indexes remain up for the year, despite the recent losses.

content.headline: Trump promotes immigration hardliner Stephen Miller to chief of staff
content.shortHeadline: Trump names Stephen Miller his new chief of staff
content.standfirst: Miller’s appointment follows the Republicans’ midterm defeat and signals no clear retreat from the president’s immigration agenda. Democrats say they will scrutinise his role as they prepare to take control of Congress.

image.caption: Stephen Miller at the White House in Washington, DC, in March 2025.

sources.originalTitle: Stephen Miller, architect of Trump’s immigration crackdown, to become White House chief of staff
With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
How Stephen Miller appointment shows Trump hasn’t learned his lesson on immigration

segments.body: Donald Trump has named Stephen Miller, his long-serving adviser and a central figure in his immigration policy, as White House chief of staff. Miller is due to start on Monday, replacing Susie Wiles, who said she would leave the role after what she called an honour to serve the president.

segments.title: A combative choice after the midterms
segments.body: The appointment came days after Republicans lost control of Congress. Miller said the mission was to “fight with all of our soul” to support Trump. The Guardian reports that immigration advocates expect the administration’s deportation drive to continue, while Democrats promise oversight and investigations.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis argues that Miller’s promotion signals a harder line on immigration despite the election result, and notes that Democrats’ ability to constrain enforcement agencies may be limited by existing funding and staffing.

segments.body: Miller’s appointment is also likely to complicate dealings with the incoming Democratic-led Congress. The BBC reports that some Republicans have criticised him too, while the Guardian records Democratic leaders’ denunciations of his record. Trump has praised Miller as an effective manager.

content.headline: EU prosecutors investigate possible misuse of funds after Spain rail disaster
content.shortHeadline: EU opens probe into rail funds after deadly Spain crash
content.standfirst: Prosecutors are examining whether EU money for safety and signalling upgrades was misused on the Madrid–Seville line, where two crashes have killed 115 people this year. The inquiry adds to pressure on Spain’s government ahead of an election.

image.caption: The October rail crash near Urda killed 69 people.

sources.originalTitle: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster

segments.body: The European Public Prosecutor’s Office has opened an investigation into possible fraud involving EU funds for railway safety, signalling and communications upgrades on Spain’s Madrid–Seville high-speed line. Investigators visited the offices of rail infrastructure authority Adif and safety agency AESF.

segments.title: A line under scrutiny
segments.body: The probe follows the 28 October crash near Urda, in which 69 people died, and a separate fatal crash on the same line in January. The two accidents have killed 115 people. The inquiry is ongoing; prosecutors have not released further details. Spain’s transport minister resigned this week, while opposition parties are demanding further accountability.

content.headline: Bomb threats disrupt European flights, including at Copenhagen Airport
content.shortHeadline: Bomb threats disrupt flights across Europe
content.standfirst: Dozens of threats against aircraft and airports have led to diversions and emergency checks, but no explosives have been found in the incidents reported. Authorities have not established who is responsible or whether the cases are connected.

image.caption: European airports and flights have faced a series of bomb threats.

source.credit: Foto: Miguel A. Lopes / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Europæisk flytrafik ramt af flere bombetrusler – men hvem står bag?
Spate of bomb threats poses serious challenge to airline industry

segments.body: Bomb threats have disrupted flights and airports across Europe this week. TV 2 reports that Copenhagen Airport was among those targeted on Friday, while Reuters figures cited by the broadcaster say 29 aircraft were affected on Thursday. The BBC reports at least 32 threats affecting a dozen airlines over four days; the incidents it describes were hoaxes.

segments.title: Who is behind the threats?
segments.body: No authorities have publicly identified a perpetrator or confirmed that the threats are linked. TV 2 reports that security analysts suspect possible Russian connections, but Danish intelligence service PET says it cannot yet determine who is behind the incidents or whether they are related. Russia has denied involvement in the events discussed in the report.

perspectives.body: TV 2’s experts point to a possible wider campaign to create fear in Europe, but PET’s position remains that responsibility and links between incidents are unconfirmed.

content.headline: EU says TikTok’s recommendation feed may breach digital rules
content.shortHeadline: EU finds TikTok feed may breach digital law
content.standfirst: The European Commission’s preliminary finding says TikTok has not adequately addressed risks from its personalised “For You” feed, including repeated exposure to material on distress and body image. The company faces a possible fine if it does not address the concerns.

sources.originalTitle: Tiktok bryder loven med "kaninhul", vurderer EU-Kommission

segments.body: The European Commission has preliminarily concluded that TikTok may be violating the Digital Services Act. Its concern is that the platform’s “For You” feed can repeatedly recommend material about sadness, isolation or body image, potentially affecting the mental health of vulnerable adults and minors.

segments.title: A preliminary finding
segments.body: The Commission says TikTok has not taken proportionate and effective steps to reduce these risks. If the company does not address the concerns, it could face a fine of up to 6% of its worldwide annual turnover. The finding is preliminary, not a final ruling.

content.headline: Houston orders police to limit cooperation with federal immigration agency
content.shortHeadline: Houston limits police cooperation with ICE
content.standfirst: Mayor John Whitmire says officers will notify immigration authorities only when a person arrested for an offence carrying possible jail time also has an administrative warrant. He says the change is intended to reduce fear after public anger over immigration enforcement.

image.caption: Houston Mayor John Whitmire has ordered a change to police cooperation with ICE.

sources.originalTitle: Texas mayor instructs police to limit cooperation with ICE

segments.body: Houston Mayor John Whitmire has directed city police to contact Immigration and Customs Enforcement only when someone arrested for a jailable offence also has an administrative ICE warrant. Previously, officers were required to notify ICE when such a warrant appeared during a database check.

segments.title: A contested change
segments.body: Whitmire says the order is intended to reduce fear in the community and follows months of anger after an ICE officer fatally shot a man in Houston. The Department of Homeland Security criticised the move, saying local cooperation is important to its enforcement work. Austin has also begun a similar policy change.

content.headline: Thomas Markle appears in court after charge over child sexual abuse material
content.shortHeadline: Thomas Markle appears in court on federal charge
content.standfirst: Meghan, Duchess of Sussex’s father was charged in the US with one count of possessing indecent images of children. No plea was taken at his first hearing; he has previously denied possessing such material.

image.caption: Thomas Markle pictured in San Diego, California, in 2018.

sources.originalTitle: Thomas Markle, Meghan’s father, charged in Florida in connection to child sexual abuse material
Meghan's father Thomas Markle appears in court over child sex abuse material
Thomas Markle charged by FBI with possession of child sexual abuse material

segments.body: Thomas Markle, 82, appeared in federal court in Tampa after being arrested in Florida and charged with one count of possessing child sexual abuse material. The court ordered him to home detention at his assisted-living facility and electronic monitoring. No plea was taken; an arraignment date in California is to be set.

segments.title: The investigation
segments.body: The FBI says it seized about 78 items from two storage units in the Los Angeles area that Markle rented. Prosecutors allege some material contained images of child sexual abuse; the FBI says its review is ongoing. Markle has previously denied possessing such images, calling the allegations “sick lies”. Meghan has said she is deeply distressed by the allegations.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that prosecutors say the investigation is ongoing and that their office has no evidence of victims in the US based on material seized so far.

content.headline: UK settlement plans leave some migrants facing longer waits and uncertainty
content.shortHeadline: Settlement changes leave migrants facing longer waits
content.standfirst: The government has kept a five-year route for some care workers, but others may have to wait longer for permanent settlement. Migrants whose family circumstances or benefit claims do not fit the stated protections say the rules remain unclear.

image.caption: Rasika Samarasinghe with his wife and children after the Home Office reversed its refusal to let them remain in the UK.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I feel free now’: Shabana Mahmood’s immigration shake-up provokes mixed emotions

segments.body: Revised settlement plans offer some qualifying care workers a five-year route, after ministers faced pressure from Labour MPs and unions. Other migrants may face a longer wait, and the government has not clarified how its protections apply to people whose relationships have ended or who have claimed benefits.

segments.title: Different effects on families
segments.body: Aneisha Williams says housing benefit could now delay her settlement after she relied on it during a period of homelessness; she says she had expected to qualify soon. Care worker Rasika Samarasinghe, by contrast, says his family can plan their future after the Home Office reversed a refusal to let his wife and children remain. Campaigners say important details are still unresolved.

content.headline: UK minister considers a separate benefits system to help young people into work
content.shortHeadline: UK weighs separate benefits system for young people
content.standfirst: Pat McFadden says he is studying Denmark’s subsidised employment model and wants a more active approach to work and training. He says any changes would be shaped by forthcoming reviews and could require legislation next year.

image.caption: Pat McFadden at an event in London highlighting youth employment schemes.

sources.originalTitle: Separate youth benefits system likely to swap cash for job support

segments.body: Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden says the government is considering a distinct benefits approach for young people, with more employment and training support rather than relying mainly on cash payments. He was speaking during a visit to Copenhagen to study Denmark’s Fleksjob scheme.

segments.title: The Danish model
segments.body: Fleksjob, introduced in 1998, allows people with health conditions or disabilities to work reduced hours with state-subsidised wages. McFadden says he is interested in a system that focuses on what people can do. He says recommendations from two reviews will inform policy, with legislation possible next year; he has not set out detailed proposals.

content.headline: UK resilience plans warn a prolonged blackout could disrupt essential services
content.shortHeadline: How the UK is preparing for a prolonged blackout
content.standfirst: A past flood-related outage in Lancaster showed how power loss can interrupt water, transport, shops and communications. The BBC is developing emergency broadcasting plans, while an engineer quoted in the report warns that some fallback systems are being phased out.

image.caption: The government’s “Be Ready” campaign advises households about severe disruption.

sources.originalTitle: What happens if all the lights go out? This is the plan for a 'Black Sky' event

segments.body: A 2015 flood in Lancaster left about 61,500 people without electricity and disrupted water supplies, transport, shops and cash machines. FM radio and copper-wire landlines were among the communications that continued to work, according to a review cited by the BBC.

segments.title: Planning for disruption
segments.body: The BBC says about 100 staff would run an emergency radio service from a studio with independent communications and supplies for at least three days. The report also notes that the UK’s copper landline network is due to be switched off in January 2027 and that the future of FM radio is under review. The government says there is no specific threat to the electricity grid.

content.headline: Russell Brand’s barrister refers himself to regulator after post-verdict outbur
content.shortHeadline: Brand barrister refers himself to professional regulator
content.standfirst: Ian Winter KC says he reported himself to the Bar Standards Board after an exchange with a journalist following Brand’s conviction. The case has also prompted criticism of courtroom arguments about how complainants respond to sexual violence.

image.caption: Ian Winter KC has referred himself to the Bar Standards Board.

sources.originalTitle: How Russell Brand’s lawyer could undermine future rape cases, according to experts

segments.body: Ian Winter KC has referred himself to the Bar Standards Board after a Sunday Times journalist said he confronted her following Russell Brand’s conviction for rape and sexual assault. Winter said his professional duty required him to report the allegations so they could be scrutinised. The regulator has not announced an outcome.

segments.title: Debate over courtroom conduct
segments.body: The i Paper reports criticism of questions asked during Brand’s trial about why complainants did not resist or report the alleged assaults sooner. Campaigners say such arguments can reinforce rape myths; a criminal barrister quoted in the report says the treatment of adult witnesses is also governed by legal expectations. Brand denied the charges and was convicted by a jury.

content.headline: Danish utilities fear unusual information requests could aid cyberattacks
content.shortHeadline: Danish utilities warn of suspicious information requests
content.standfirst: Water and district-heating companies say they have received a wave of unusual requests, some apparently generated by AI. The sender and motive are unknown, and industry groups fear the inquiries could be used to map critical infrastructure.

image.caption: Danish utilities say they have received unusual requests for information about their operations.

sources.originalTitle: 'Mærkelige' anmodninger rammer mange forsyningsselskaber: Branche frygter, det kan bruges til et cyberangreb

segments.body: Danish water and district-heating companies have received an unusual volume of requests for information in recent weeks. Industry groups say some appear to be AI-generated and ask about court cases or people who do not exist in the companies’ records. The sender and motive have not been established.

segments.title: A wider pattern, still unverified
segments.body: Utilities fear the requests could help someone learn how critical services are organised, but no attack has been confirmed. The report says educational institutions have also received unusual requests, raising similar concerns about access to sensitive data. Industry representatives want clearer official guidance on how to handle requests while meeting their legal duties.

perspectives.body: The water-sector group DANVA says requests look less suspicious in isolation, but the fact that other parts of critical infrastructure report similar activity makes the pattern concerning. Authorities had not answered DR’s questions by Friday.

content.headline: Danish prosecutors examine whether to reopen case over British woman’s death
content.shortHeadline: Danish prosecutors review whether to reopen Leeson case
content.standfirst: Police are examining whether Don McPherson can be prosecuted in Denmark over his wife Paula Leeson’s 2017 death, despite his acquittal in a British criminal trial. No decision has been made, and the legal bar to a new prosecution remains unclear.

image.caption: Paula Leeson died in a swimming pool at a holiday home in Houstrup in 2017.

sources.originalTitle: Dansk anklager overvejer at genoptage sag om britisk millionarvings død

segments.body: South and Southern Jutland Police say they are examining whether the criminal case over Paula Leeson’s death can be reopened in Denmark. Her husband, Don McPherson, was acquitted of murder in a 2021 British trial. Danish prosecutors say a person acquitted abroad generally cannot be prosecuted for the same offence elsewhere, but they are assessing the legal position.

segments.title: Evidence and unresolved questions
segments.body: New evidence emerged in a later British civil case, including data from Leeson’s fitness watch indicating she drowned before McPherson retrieved her from a swimming pool. A civil judge and a British coroner found that she was murdered, but these findings are not a criminal conviction. The British prosecution service declined a retrial, saying the watch evidence had been available at the original trial but was not used.

perspectives.body: Leeson’s family is urging Danish prosecutors to act. Police have acknowledged that the original Danish investigation may have missed opportunities to examine details more fully, but have not said whether a new prosecution is legally possible.

content.headline: Danish MP appeals three-year ban over company bankruptcy
content.shortHeadline: MP appeals three-year bankruptcy ban
content.standfirst: Independent MP Jacob Harris is appealing a court-imposed ban linked to his work with a company that went bankrupt. The ban will not take effect while the appeal proceeds; Harris says he believes the truth will prevail.

image.caption: Jacob Harris was elected to parliament in March and is now an independent MP.

sources.originalTitle: Jacob Harris vil tage sag om konkurskarantæne til landsretten

segments.body: Independent member of parliament Jacob Harris has appealed a three-year bankruptcy restriction imposed by the bankruptcy court in Roskilde. The ruling means he would be barred from managing or sitting on the board of a company, but the restriction does not take effect while his appeal is under way.

segments.title: The court’s findings
segments.body: The restriction relates to Krokodille ApS, which went bankrupt. The court cited incomplete bookkeeping, including the absence of records for 2025. Harris’s wife, who was also given a three-year restriction, is appealing too. Harris was elected for Borgernes Parti in March and became an independent after the party expelled him.

content.headline: Government allies clash over who should own Denmark’s proposed SU cuts
content.shortHeadline: Danish coalition allies clash over student grant cuts
content.standfirst: Moderate Party finance spokesman Lars Aagaard says Socialist People’s Party should take responsibility for student grant cuts it agreed to in government. SF says it accepts the compromise but rejects the idea that the cuts are its own policy.

image.caption: Moderate Party finance spokesman Lars Aagaard has criticised SF over student grant cuts.

sources.originalTitle: Moderaterne til SF: 'Tør øjnene eller træd ud af regeringen'

segments.body: Lars Aagaard of the Moderate Party has told coalition partner SF to “dry your eyes or leave the government” over proposed cuts to student grants. He argues that SF must own measures it accepted as part of a government compromise.

segments.title: SF says it accepts the compromise
segments.body: SF says the cuts were not its idea, but that entering government means making compromises. The party says taking responsibility for an agreement does not make every part of it SF policy. The other government parties did not identify who first proposed the cuts.

perspectives.body: Aagaard argues that SF is presenting only part of the bargain to students: he says the party should explain what it accepted the grant changes in exchange for.

content.headline: Danish animal-rescue group expects another record year for deer collisions
content.shortHeadline: Deer collisions in Denmark may hit another record
content.standfirst: Animal Protection says rising deer numbers, more traffic and expanding roads may be contributing to collisions, which are especially common around dawn and dusk in autumn. The report gives two different totals for 2025, so the exact comparison is unclear.

image.caption: Leif Stonor Nielsen, a trained tracking-dog handler, searches for injured deer.

sources.originalTitle: Pas på: 'Helt vildt' mange dyr bliver påkørt lige nu

segments.body: Animal Protection expects the number of deer struck by vehicles in Denmark to set another record this year. Its biologist says more deer, more cars and road expansion may all contribute. Collisions peak in October and November, when deer are active at the same time many people travel to and from work.

segments.title: What drivers can do
segments.body: The report urges drivers to slow down near deer-warning signs, which mark places with higher collision risk. People who strike a deer can call Animal Protection’s 1812 line: a marksman may be sent if the animal is still at the roadside, or a tracking dog if it has run off.

content.headline: Everton fight back to beat Coventry 3-1 as Dewsbury-Hall responds to England sn,
content.shortHeadline: Everton rally past Coventry as Dewsbury-Hall scores
content.standfirst: Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall marked his England omission with a late goal as Everton came from behind to beat Coventry 3-1. Thierno Barry scored twice, lifting Everton to fifth in the Premier League.

image.caption: Thierno Barry scores twice as Everton fight back to beat Coventry.

sources.originalTitle: England 'disappointment' fuels Dewsbury-Hall's Everton heroics
Lampard feels hair pull should have led to Coventry penalty

segments.body: Everton recovered from Yann Gboho’s second-half opener to beat Coventry 3-1 at Hill Dickinson Stadium. Thierno Barry scored twice in five minutes to turn the game around, before Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall sealed the win with a late strike.

segments.title: Coventry dispute key decisions
segments.body: Coventry manager Frank Lampard felt his side should have had a penalty after James Tarkowski pulled Caleb Yirenkyi’s hair, and also questioned a possible handball in the build-up to Barry’s second goal. Everton manager David Moyes disagreed over the handball and said the hair-pulling rule needed addressing.

perspectives.body: Lampard said the hair pull should have been a foul and argued that the decisions could have changed the game. The match report’s analysis considered Coventry had grounds to feel aggrieved over two of the calls.

content.headline: Ireland beat Argentina 42-12 but Farrell says they missed a chance to be more
content.shortHeadline: Ireland win big but Farrell wants greater ruthlessness
content.standfirst: Hugo Keenan’s hat-trick helped Ireland begin their home Nations Championship campaign with a six-try win. Andy Farrell praised the performance but said his side could have made more of their territorial dominance.

image.caption: Ireland celebrate during their win over Argentina.

sources.originalTitle: Keenan hat-trick as six-try Ireland beat Pumas
Six tries and a big win - but were Ireland ruthless?

segments.body: Ireland beat Argentina 42-12 in Dublin, with Hugo Keenan scoring three tries and Dan Sheehan, Sam Prendergast and Ronan Kelleher also crossing. The win puts Ireland top of the northern hemisphere table before the weekend’s other matches.

segments.title: A win with room to improve
segments.body: Ireland did not score after the 55th minute despite having 59% of the territory. Farrell said they had missed a chance to be ruthless, while Tadhg Beirne also felt they had not capitalised on late opportunities. Captain Sheehan went off after failing a head injury assessment, and several other players had injury concerns.

perspectives.body: Farrell said the scoreline was good but the story was Ireland’s missed chance to be more ruthless. He also highlighted the injuries to Sheehan, Robert Baloucoune, Sean Jansen, Josh van der Flier and Mack Hansen.

content.headline: Alcaraz saves two match points to beat Fritz and help Jodar reach ATP Finals
content.shortHeadline: Alcaraz saves two match points in Paris win
content.standfirst: Carlos Alcaraz recovered from a set down to beat Taylor Fritz in the Paris Masters quarter-finals. The result also secured Rafael Jodar’s place at the season-ending ATP Finals.

image.caption: Carlos Alcaraz, who saved two match points to beat Taylor Fritz in Paris.

sources.originalTitle: Alcaraz beats Fritz to help Jodar reach ATP finals

segments.body: Alcaraz saved two match points before beating Fritz 6-7 (10-12) 7-5 6-3. After dropping the first set and falling behind by a break in the second, the Spaniard rallied to take control of the decider and reach the semi-finals.

The victory ended Fritz’s hopes of qualifying for the ATP Finals and secured a place at the event for fellow Spaniard Rafael Jodar. Jodar, 20, will make his debut at the season-ending tournament in Turin.

content.headline: McIlroy fires 63 to move within one shot of the Abu Dhabi lead
content.shortHeadline: McIlroy’s 63 puts him one shot off the lead
content.standfirst: Rory McIlroy carded 11 birdies in a nine-under-par second round to move to 11 under, one shot behind the shared lead. It followed a two-shot penalty in his opening round.

image.caption: Rory McIlroy is chasing a sixth successive Race to Dubai crown.

sources.originalTitle: McIlroy fires 63 to move into Abu Dhabi contention

segments.body: McIlroy shot a nine-under-par 63 on Friday to reach 11 under overall at the Abu Dhabi Championship. Jon Rahm, Tyrell Hatton and Francesco Laporta share the lead on 12 under; McIlroy is among four players one shot behind.

The six-time major winner had started the day eight shots back after a two-shot penalty for improving his lie during the first round. He said he had made peace with the penalty and felt able to focus on his golf, adding that he saw encouraging signs with his putting.

content.headline: Scotland look to turn last year’s narrow All Blacks defeat into a first win
content.shortHeadline: Scotland seek a historic first win over New Zealand
content.standfirst: Scotland get another chance to beat New Zealand, a team they have never defeated in 121 years of meetings. Captain Sione Tuipulotu says the side has grown through a difficult year and learned from last season’s narrow loss.

image.caption: Scotland captain Sione Tuipulotu leads his side against New Zealand.

sources.originalTitle: Scotland come full circle for another crack at All Blacks

segments.body: Scotland meet the All Blacks at Murrayfield on Saturday, still seeking their first win over New Zealand. In last year’s meeting, Scotland came back from 17-0 to level the match before losing 25-17 to a late Damien McKenzie try.

segments.title: Lessons from a turbulent year
segments.body: Tuipulotu said Scotland had progressed through both landmark wins and difficult defeats. Since last year’s meeting, they have beaten England and France and pushed world champions South Africa close, but the captain said the challenge is to sustain their best rugby for longer.

content.headline: Khawaja says Australia’s whole team knew of 2018 ball-tampering
content.shortHeadline: Khawaja says Australia’s whole team knew of sandpaper use
content.standfirst: In extracts from his autobiography, Usman Khawaja says the whole team knew about sandpaper being used to alter the ball in the 2018 South Africa series. Four bowlers, including Pat Cummins, have previously denied prior knowledge.

image.caption: Usman Khawaja, who has made claims about Australia’s 2018 ball-tampering scandal.

sources.originalTitle: Whole Australia team knew of sandpaper use - Khawaja

segments.body: Usman Khawaja says discussions about tampering with the ball began during the second Test of Australia’s 2018 series in South Africa. In extracts from his autobiography, he says the team knew about the use of sandpaper in the third Test at Cape Town, where Cameron Bancroft was caught on camera.

segments.title: Bowlers have denied prior knowledge
segments.body: Khawaja says the team should have taken collective responsibility and that he was shocked not to be asked to provide evidence during Cricket Australia’s investigation. Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon said in 2021 that they did not know a foreign substance had been taken onto the field.

content.headline: Afghan women cricketers criticise overseas signings for men’s league
content.shortHeadline: Afghan women say rights matter more than any league
content.standfirst: Afghan women’s players say overseas cricketers joining the planned Afghanistan Premier League risk ignoring the exclusion of women and girls from sport. The men’s league is expected to start in the UAE but has not been sanctioned by the ICC.

image.caption: Afghan women’s cricketers Firooza Amiri and Nahida Sapan.

sources.originalTitle: Women's rights matter more than any league, say Afghan cricketers

segments.body: Afghan women’s cricketers have criticised foreign players who signed for the planned men’s Afghanistan Premier League. Nahida Sapan said their participation could send a message that the suffering of Afghan women and girls can be ignored; women’s participation in sport has been effectively outlawed since the Taliban returned to power in 2021.

segments.title: Players call for scrutiny
segments.body: Firooza Amiri said she was not asking international players to turn their backs on Afghanistan, but to distinguish support for its people from legitimising a system that has taken away women’s rights. Eight English players were signed in the draft, and the league is yet to receive ICC sanction.

content.headline: Jobe Bellingham earns first England call-up as Palmer is left out
content.shortHeadline: Jobe Bellingham called up as Palmer misses England squad
content.standfirst: Jobe Bellingham has earned his first senior England call-up after establishing himself at Borussia Dortmund. Cole Palmer was left out, with Thomas Tuchel saying the Chelsea forward has missed too many opportunities to impress.

image.caption: Jude and Jobe Bellingham could become the first brothers to play together for England since the Neville brothers.

sources.originalTitle: 'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up
Is Palmer's England career over under Tuchel?

segments.body: Jobe Bellingham, 21, has been called into England’s senior squad for the first time. Tuchel said the midfielder had earned the opportunity through his performances at Dortmund, where he has become a regular, and described the call-up as an achievement for the family.

segments.title: Palmer faces a fight to return
segments.body: Palmer was omitted despite being checked for fitness before the squad was named. Tuchel said Palmer “misses too many opportunities to impress” and that competition for places is open. Palmer has 14 England caps, but has featured in only three of Tuchel’s 26 matches in charge.

content.headline: U2 on 50 years together, their new album and why Bono won’t work with Trump
content.shortHeadline: U2 on 50 years together and a new album
content.standfirst: As U2 prepare to release Carnaval de Luz and return to touring, the four bandmates discuss their long-running shared decision-making, the music that brought them back into focus and why Bono says the Trump administration calls for a different response.

image.caption: Bono with U2 bandmates Larry Mullen, Adam Clayton and the Edge.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s a new world. It’s a little fascistic. And it needs a different response’: U2 on 50 years together – and why Bono can’t work with Trump

segments.body: U2 are marking 50 years since Larry Mullen put a notice on his school board seeking musicians, with a new album and world tour on the way. In an interview, the four members look back on the band’s unlikely longevity and the shared songwriting credits and committee decisions Bono calls “the soviet”.

segments.title: A different moment
segments.body: The group say Carnaval de Luz, their first album of new material in nearly nine years, aims to sound like music only U2 could make. It includes a duet with Dolly Parton and a song about Rosalía. Bono says he has been invited to meet the Trump administration but does not feel equipped to negotiate with it, describing the political climate as different from earlier encounters with US leaders.

content.headline: Clem Cattini, drummer behind more than 40 UK number-one singles, dies at 86
content.shortHeadline: Clem Cattini, drummer on more than 40 No 1s, dies at 86
content.standfirst: Largely unknown outside the music business, Cattini was a highly sought-after session drummer whose playing featured on hits by Dusty Springfield, the Walker Brothers and many others.

image.caption: Clem Cattini with the Tornados in 1963.

sources.originalTitle: Clem Cattini obituary

segments.body: Clem Cattini played on more than 40 UK number-one singles over a career spanning 45 years, the Guardian reports. A leading session drummer, he worked with artists including Dusty Springfield, the Walker Brothers, the Kinks, Paul McCartney and Lou Reed. He has died aged 86; the obituary does not state a cause of death.

segments.title: A working musician
segments.body: Cattini first found success as a band member, drumming on Johnny Kidd and the Pirates’ “Shakin’ All Over” and the Tornados’ “Telstar”. He later became a dependable studio musician, sometimes recording several sessions in a day. He called himself a “musical navvy” and said he was not ashamed to play on any kind of record: “In the end it was all just work.”

content.headline: Spice Girls’ 30th-anniversary box set offers fans little new for a high price
content.shortHeadline: Spice Girls’ pricey anniversary set offers little new
content.standfirst: The 160-track collection follows reunion hints that raised fans’ hopes, but much of its material has already been repackaged. The Guardian review finds the strongest case for it in a previously unreleased song featuring Victoria Beckham on lead vocals.

image.caption: The Spice Girls during their 1990s heyday.

sources.originalTitle: Spice Girls: The Singles Collection review – stop fleecing your fans right now, thank you very much

segments.body: After social-media teasers suggested a reunion might be in the works, the Spice Girls announced a 30th-anniversary box set instead: 14 CDs and 160 tracks, priced at £94.99, or a 7-inch vinyl edition at £179.99. The Guardian review argues that the release asks a lot of fans when much of its older material has appeared in earlier anniversary collections.

segments.title: A worthwhile curio
segments.body: The collection’s main novelty is “Do You Think About Me”, a song recorded when the group were called Touch. Victoria Beckham takes the lead, sounding confident on the R&B-tinged ballad. The review also finds pleasure in the original singles and some B-sides, but says the volume of remixes and repeated reissues leave the new material feeling slight.

content.headline: Wynonna Judd’s new album turns family loss and personal struggle into song
content.shortHeadline: Wynonna Judd puts a lifetime of pain into a new album
content.standfirst: On The Hard Truth, the country singer leaves behind polished Nashville production for raw songs shaped by grief and decades of upheaval. She describes making the record as part of her own healing.

image.caption: Wynonna Judd.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I went into a deep, deep hole’: Wynonna Judd on overcoming family tragedy and putting a lifetime of love and pain into her new album

segments.body: Wynonna Judd’s first album in a decade, The Hard Truth, trades slick Nashville production for a pared-back blend of country, blues and soul. Judd co-wrote nearly every track, drawing on her struggles and the death of her mother, Naomi, who died by suicide in 2022. “Making this record was my approach to healing,” she says.

segments.title: Songs from a family history
segments.body: The opening song addresses Judd’s mother directly, while other tracks draw on the late discovery of her biological father’s identity and her concerns for her adult daughter, who is living with addiction. Judd says she is raising her granddaughter. The interview also recalls her childhood in poverty and the Judds’ success as a mother-and-daughter country duo.

content.headline: Enrico Rava and Joe Lovano find fresh possibilities in jazz on Corners
content.shortHeadline: Enrico Rava and Joe Lovano’s jazz dialogues take risks
content.standfirst: The 87-year-old Italian trumpeter’s new album moves between late-Miles funk, free improvisation and lyrical ballads. The Guardian review highlights a set that balances restless exchanges with a striking vocal contribution from drummer Evita Polidoro.

image.caption: Enrico Rava and members of the Fearless Five with Joe Lovano.

sources.originalTitle: Enrico Rava Fearless Five with Joe Lovano: Corners review – daring dialogues from 87-year-old Miles Davis disciple

segments.body: On Corners, Enrico Rava plays with his Fearless Five group and longtime friend Joe Lovano. The Guardian review hears the 87-year-old trumpeter drawing on Miles Davis while pushing beyond linear post-bop, bringing together funk, free improvisation, brass harmonies and melody.

segments.title: Room for new voices
segments.body: The review singles out drummer and vocalist Evita Polidoro’s “Le Mie Gambe” as a personal, carefully paced performance, and notes the album’s shifts from Lovano’s free improvisation to trumpet-and-guitar exchanges. It also recommends new releases by Tamar Osborn, Moses Boyd, and Bill Laurance and Michael League.

content.headline: Laila! weighs the promise and anxiety of young adulthood on her second album
content.shortHeadline: Laila! reflects on time and change in a lush second album
content.standfirst: The New York songwriter’s record follows the jump from school to independent adulthood, holding gratitude and unease in the same frame. Pitchfork finds its strongest moments in songs that make possibility feel vivid.

sources.originalTitle: We’ll Never Be This Young Again

segments.body: Laila! released her debut album, Gap Year!, at 18. Two years later, after graduating, touring and moving into her first adult apartment, she returns with We’ll Never Be This Young Again, an album about the excitement of new possibilities and the anxiety of feeling time pass.

segments.title: Where the feeling lands
segments.body: Pitchfork finds the title song’s reflections on youth relatively flat, but praises “Better Days”, a ballad about lost love, and “Anything Can Happen”, whose bright synths and airy vocals evoke an expanding sense of opportunity. Laila! produced nearly every track, aiming for a seamless, immersive sound.

content.headline: June McDoom brings Jamaican mento heritage into her debut album, Follow theLight
content.shortHeadline: June McDoom blends mento and folk on Follow the Light
content.standfirst: The singer draws on her grandfather’s mento playing and her own love of folk to make an album that brings Jamaican musical history into conversation with dub and psychedelia.

sources.originalTitle: Follow the Light

segments.body: June McDoom’s debut, Follow the Light, draws on the Jamaican mento music she heard her grandfather Colin Smith play at family gatherings, as well as the folk records she loved growing up. Pitchfork describes the album as a fresh engagement with a style that has become less prominent in Caribbean popular music.

segments.title: Tradition in motion
segments.body: Working with collaborator Evan Wright, McDoom combines voice and nylon-string guitar with flute, strings, synths, dub bass and echo. The review highlights “Dream Dub” for the way its rhythm section drops away and returns around her voice, and “Grandpa”, which includes a voice note from her grandfather.

content.headline: Amy Winehouse’s Back to Black anniversary set adds demos but leaves little to re
content.shortHeadline: Back to Black’s anniversary set adds demos, not a new chapter
content.standfirst: The expanded edition gathers a handful of previously unheard tracks alongside live recordings and B-sides, but Pitchfork argues the original album remains the centrepiece—and that no collection can fill the gaps in Winehouse’s short catalogue.

image.caption: Amy Winehouse, whose album Back to Black was released in 2006.

sources.originalTitle: Back to Black (20th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The 20th-anniversary edition of Amy Winehouse’s Back to Black includes five previously unheard tracks, alongside demos, B-sides and a full Amsterdam concert recording. Pitchfork says the new versions reveal how the album developed from a neo-soul sound toward its final, retro-styled production.

segments.title: What an archive can’t restore
segments.body: The review calls Back to Black a landmark breakup album, praising the way Winehouse’s personal writing meets a sound drawing on Motown, doo-wop and contemporary hip-hop. The additional material is welcome, but the review notes that the planned follow-up’s demos were destroyed and argues that the anniversary package cannot fill that absence.

content.headline: Florence Pugh’s Star Wars comparison raises questions about Dune’s vision of a“s
content.shortHeadline: Is Dune really this generation’s Star Wars?
content.standfirst: Florence Pugh calls Denis Villeneuve’s saga a generational Star Wars, but the Guardian argues the franchises imagine very different kinds of heroes. The comparison becomes more unsettling as Dune’s next chapter approaches.

image.caption: Timothée Chalamet and Rebecca Ferguson in Dune.

sources.originalTitle: If Dune is this generation’s Star Wars, we are all in big trouble

segments.body: Florence Pugh has described Dune as her generation’s Star Wars, praising the films for making cinema feel like an event. The Guardian essay questions the comparison: Star Wars offers a rebellion against tyranny and the possibility of redemption, while Dune follows Paul Atreides toward power and the danger of a ruler who may foresee catastrophe without stopping it.

segments.title: A spectacle with a warning
segments.body: The essay grants Villeneuve’s films a striking visual scale, from vast ships and armies in the desert to the arrival of sandworms. It suggests the comparison may make sense in a darker way: Dune’s spectacle places viewers inside a story about a powerful man whose ascent could bring disaster.

content.headline: The Cat in the Hat review: Bill Hader can’t rescue a corporate, overlong reboot
content.shortHeadline: Bill Hader brightens a messy Cat in the Hat reboot
content.standfirst: Hader and Matt Berry bring energy to this animated adaptation, but the Guardian finds the film overlong and short on imagination. Its corporate lessons, the review argues, sit uneasily with Dr Seuss’s anarchic spirit.

image.caption: The Cat in the Hat in the 2026 animated film.

sources.originalTitle: The Cat in the Hat review – Bill Hader brings plenty but this animated rework is a mess

segments.body: Bill Hader voices the Cat in the Hat in a big-budget animated reboot that sends the character to cheer up two children after a family move. The Guardian review finds Hader’s performance and Matt Berry’s talking goldfish among the highlights, but says the film’s setup and adventure are painfully stretched.

segments.title: Whimsy meets the workplace
segments.body: The review criticises the film for borrowing familiar animated-film touches and turning Seussian mischief into a story about jobs, landlords and career planning. It sees the result as an exhausting attempt to serve all ages, with corporate themes crowding out the source material’s wordplay and unruliness.

content.headline: Rocky at 50: Stallone’s underdog story remains an exhilarating contender
content.shortHeadline: Rocky still packs a punch 50 years later
content.standfirst: The 1976 film has clear roots in darker boxing dramas, but its scrappy Philadelphia story finds a fresh, rousing idealism. The Guardian revisits a performance and film that remain compelling on their anniversary.

image.caption: Sylvester Stallone as Rocky Balboa.

sources.originalTitle: Rocky review – 50 years on, Stallone’s boxer remains an exhilaratingly gritty contender

segments.body: The Guardian revisits Rocky for its 50th anniversary, describing Sylvester Stallone’s story of a working-class Philadelphia boxer as an idealistic answer to boxing films steeped in defeat and cynicism. Rocky’s chance to fight world champion Apollo Creed gives the film its underdog plot, but its emotional centre is his relationship with Adrian.

segments.title: The moral victory
segments.body: The review praises John G. Avildsen’s unhurried direction and Stallone’s convincing presence in the ring. Rocky’s achievement is not simply winning a fight: the film finds its resolution in his determination to go the distance and in the personal connection he makes, offering a hopeful contrast with the genre’s more tragic traditions.

content.headline: Christy Carlson Romano on Disney fame, family pressures and finding her own way
content.shortHeadline: Christy Carlson Romano reflects on child stardom and its cost
content.standfirst: The former Even Stevens star describes the pressure to please adults, difficult family dynamics and the struggle to build a life after early success. She says the industry needs stronger mental-health support for young performers.

image.caption: Christy Carlson Romano.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Mom encouraged me to get breast implants’: Disney child star Christy Carlson Romano on fame, family and freedom

segments.body: Christy Carlson Romano began acting at six and became a Disney star in Even Stevens. In an interview about her memoir, Once Upon a Trainwreck, she describes how being praised as a “good girl” reinforced her compliance, and how a career that took her away from home made it hard to feel like an ordinary child.

segments.title: Life after the spotlight
segments.body: Romano says she faced narrow expectations about her appearance and was encouraged by her mother to get breast implants for adult roles. She also recounts sexual assault, financial trouble and unhealthy relationships, and says she is now more at peace after returning to college, building a social-media career and taking on new acting work. These are her account and recollections.

content.headline: Cristian Mungiu on Fjord, a Palme d’Or winner that divides audiences
content.shortHeadline: Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord refuses easy answers
content.standfirst: The Romanian director’s drama follows a family caught between conservative religious beliefs and Norway’s child-protection system. Mungiu says he wants viewers to question their assumptions; the film’s reception shows that audiences disagree on what it is asking.

image.caption: Cristian Mungiu with Fjord stars Renate Reinsve and Sebastian Stan at Cannes.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Too many stories exist only to make you think you’re on the right side’: Cristian Mungiu on Fjord, the Cannes winner that divided Europe

segments.body: Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord follows a Romanian-Norwegian family after child-protection services investigate bruises on their eldest daughter. As the parents’ children are taken into care, the film sets their evangelical beliefs against the liberal values of their Norwegian neighbours without fully explaining how the bruises occurred.

segments.title: A film that divides
segments.body: Mungiu says he wanted to make a story that does not tell viewers who the good and bad people are. The film won the Palme d’Or, but its reception has differed: some Romanian critics say it is too forgiving of corporal punishment, while a French critic argued that it ultimately takes sides against child-protection officers. Mungiu rejects the idea that he is endorsing conservative values.

content.headline: Wicker review: Olivia Colman’s strange, sexist fairy tale is hard to resist
content.shortHeadline: Wicker is a sexist fairy tale with an irresistible oddness
content.standfirst: A woman commissions a husband made of willow in this bawdy fantasy starring Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård. The i Paper review finds its gender politics troubling, even as its absurd premise and comic energy win it over.

image.caption: Olivia Colman’s Fisherwoman with the husband woven from wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it

segments.body: In Wicker, Olivia Colman plays a fisherwoman who pays a basketmaker to create a husband from willow. Alexander Skarsgård’s wicker figure is devoted to her, unsettling a village built around unequal relationships. The i Paper review calls the result hilarious and horny, but questions a story that gives the husband little agency.

segments.title: Fantasy and fairness
segments.body: The review argues that the film’s gender reversal would be harder to accept if the roles were swapped, and worries about its message of unquestioning devotion. But it also finds something satisfying in the fisherwoman’s relief at a partner who treats her with kindness and respects her work. Its verdict: go for the laughs, not the lecture.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning review: a chilling Facebook story that leads back to us
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning puts Facebook under scrutiny
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up shifts from Facebook’s origins to reporting on its effects, including the platform’s role in political misinformation and teen mental health. The i Paper critic finds it alarming—and recognises how easily viewers return to scrolling.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling

segments.body: The Social Reckoning, written and directed by Aaron Sorkin, dramatises journalist Jeff Horwitz’s reporting on the Facebook Files and whistleblower Frances Haugen. The i Paper review describes a tense, investigative story about the platform’s influence on teen mental health and the spread of political misinformation.

segments.title: After the warning
segments.body: The review’s unease is personal as well as political: its writer says the film left them frightened, but they returned to Meta platforms that are part of daily life. It argues that repeated revelations can make people numb to the harms they describe, even as the company’s user base and influence grow.

content.headline: Elke Sommer, star of A Shot in the Dark, dies aged 85
content.shortHeadline: Elke Sommer, star of A Shot in the Dark, dies at 85
content.standfirst: The German actor became a familiar face in 1960s films, most notably as Maria Gambrelli opposite Peter Sellers in the Inspector Clouseau comedy. Her obituary also traces the limits imposed by the industry’s fixation on her looks.

image.caption: Elke Sommer and Peter Sellers in A Shot in the Dark.

sources.originalTitle: Elke Sommer obituary

segments.body: Elke Sommer, who has died aged 85, was part of a postwar wave of European actors who found work in Hollywood. Her best-known role was Maria Gambrelli in the 1964 comedy A Shot in the Dark, opposite Peter Sellers as Inspector Clouseau. The obituary recalls her flair for improvisation and her ability to hold her own in comedies.

segments.title: Beyond the ingénue roles
segments.body: Sommer spoke seven languages and worked across European and American films, television, theatre and music. She later said she had too often been treated as decoration, as roles focused on her appearance. After her Hollywood career slowed, she appeared in European films and television, including a series about painting.

content.headline: The Assassin season two review: Keeley Hawes shines as the drama loses its way
content.shortHeadline: Keeley Hawes can’t save The Assassin’s second season
content.standfirst: Hawes returns as a sardonic midlife assassin, but the Guardian finds the show’s central mother-son pairing increasingly frustrating. Its convoluted plots are less of a problem than the sitcom-style bickering that crowds out its lead character.

image.caption: Keeley Hawes and Freddie Highmore in The Assassin.

sources.originalTitle: The Assassin review – will anybody save Keeley Hawes from this unbearably pathetic boy?

segments.body: The Assassin returns with Keeley Hawes as Julie Green, a professional killer, and Freddie Highmore as her anxious son Edward. The Guardian review says the first season’s conspiracy plot at least gave the pair a maze to navigate; the new season’s wedding, kidnapping and pursuit offer more twists without strengthening the central relationship.

segments.title: A lead character left thin
segments.body: The review’s main complaint is Edward’s repeated pleading for Julie to avoid violence, even as danger closes in. Hawes remains compelling, but the script gives little attention to what being a menopausal, lone-wolf assassin might mean for Julie, instead leaning on quips and bickering.

content.headline: Rise of the Rockstar Chef serves up Ramsay and Marco Pierre White’s feud
content.shortHeadline: Ramsay and Marco Pierre White serve up kitchen history
content.standfirst: The docuseries traces the rise of British restaurant culture through the careers and rivalry of Gordon Ramsay and Marco Pierre White, with Heston Blumenthal also in the mix. The Guardian calls it gossip-rich, entertaining television, while noting its narrow focus.

image.caption: Heston Blumenthal, Gordon Ramsay and Marco Pierre White in Rise of the Rockstar Chef.

sources.originalTitle: Rise of the Rockstar Chef review – Gordon Ramsay and Marco Pierre White serve up the most sizzling TV of the year

segments.body: Rise of the Rockstar Chef revisits how Gordon Ramsay, Marco Pierre White and Heston Blumenthal helped reshape the British restaurant scene. The Guardian review finds the most compelling material in the volatile history between Ramsay and White, from restaurant rivalries to the long-awaited reunion.

segments.title: Ambition and its costs
segments.body: The series mixes career stories with accounts of feuds, kitchen rows and restaurant lore. It also considers the aggressive working cultures behind the chefs’ pursuit of perfection. The review sees a portrait of a generation that challenged the establishment and eventually became part of it, though Blumenthal is often left in the background.

content.headline: Awkwafina learns her family’s restaurant history in The Unlikely Cook
content.shortHeadline: Awkwafina reconnects with her family’s restaurant roots
content.standfirst: The series follows Nora Lum as she learns to cook and plans a pop-up honouring her family’s former Queens restaurant. The Guardian finds its most moving thread in a wider story of immigrant businesses and the grandchildren choosing to carry them on.

image.caption: Nora Lum at the Culinary Institute of America in Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook.

sources.originalTitle: Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook review – the heir to a legendary eatery … who sets soup on fire

segments.body: In Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook, Nora Lum—known professionally as Awkwafina—sets out to learn kitchen skills and create a pop-up inspired by Lum’s, the Queens restaurant founded by her great-grandfather. The Guardian review enjoys her genuine bafflement in the kitchen, though it finds some scripted jokes less convincing.

segments.title: What a restaurant carries
segments.body: As Lum visits cooks and restaurants across the US, the series explores how immigrant families introduced and adapted their food while often hoping their children would find less demanding work. The review sees the planned pop-up as part of a newer generation choosing to return to family food businesses. Lum’s 91-year-old grandmother, Powah, makes it to opening night and tells her, “I am proud of you.”

content.headline: Seven shows to stream this week, from Rivals to a Zurich bank heist
content.shortHeadline: What to stream: Rivals, 12 12 12 and more
content.standfirst: A returning bonkbuster, an elaborate heist and new seasons of familiar dramas lead this week’s picks. The Guardian’s guide also ranges from City of God to a Peanuts Christmas special.

image.caption: Bella Maclean and Alex Hassell in Rivals.

sources.originalTitle: Rivals to 12 12 12: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The Guardian’s streaming guide leads with Rivals, returning to its mix of grief, scandal and sexual politics after Monica’s death. The week’s other highlighted release, 12 12 12, follows a Zurich bank robbery through its year of planning, 12 hours of execution and 12 days of police work.

segments.title: More to browse
segments.body: Other picks include the second season of City of God, a new chapter in The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power, and two true-crime series. For lighter viewing, the guide recommends a new Peanuts animation built around Snoopy’s attempt to get off Santa’s naughty list.

content.headline: Monty Don says goodbye to Gardeners’ World in tonight’s TV picks
content.shortHeadline: Tonight: Monty Don’s Gardeners’ World farewell
content.standfirst: After more than two decades, Monty Don presents his final episode of Gardeners’ World. The Guardian’s evening guide also previews drama War, an investigation into contract killings and other viewing choices.

image.caption: Monty Don on Gardeners’ World.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: Monty Don says goodbye to Gardeners’ World after two decades

segments.body: Monty Don hangs up his trowel in his final Gardeners’ World episode after more than two decades on the programme. The Guardian’s TV guide expects a bittersweet farewell, while noting that the garden’s seasonal work carries on.

segments.title: Other viewing tonight
segments.body: The guide also recommends War, a divorce drama approaching its courtroom endgame, and an investigation into contract killers targeting whistleblowers in South Africa. Its streaming pick is Possible Love, Lee Chang-dong’s drama about class, work and the lives hidden behind ordinary appearances.

content.headline: Seven films to watch on TV this week, from Being Heumann to Avedon
content.shortHeadline: This week on TV: Being Heumann, Avedon and more
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s viewing guide ranges from a drama about disability rights activist Judy Heumann to a documentary about photographer Richard Avedon, alongside classic comedy, thriller and science fiction.

image.caption: Ruth Madeley as Judy Heumann in Being Heumann.

sources.originalTitle: Being Heumann to Avedon: the seven best films to watch on TV this week

segments.body: The guide recommends Being Heumann, with Ruth Madeley as disability rights activist Judy Heumann and a coalition of campaigners who occupied a San Francisco federal building in 1977. It describes the film as an energising account of a fight for equality that is not over.

segments.title: From classics to new arrivals
segments.body: Other selections include François Truffaut’s The Bride Wore Black, Billy Wilder’s Some Like It Hot and a documentary about photographer Richard Avedon. The guide also points to a space-station thriller, a near-future London drama and a colourful spy caper starring Monica Vitti.

content.headline: Stick season two review: Owen Wilson’s golf comedy is a warm delight
content.shortHeadline: Stick’s second season makes a warm return
content.standfirst: Pryce Cahill takes another run at the golf circuit as the show’s found family faces change. The Guardian praises Owen Wilson’s easy charm and the series’ tender reflections on regret, fatherhood and the paths not taken.

image.caption: Rhea Seehorn and Owen Wilson in Stick.

sources.originalTitle: Stick review – you really need Owen Wilson’s beautiful golf comedy in your life

segments.body: Stick returns with Pryce Cahill, played by Owen Wilson, trying to revive his golf career at 55. His young protégé Santi is pursuing a path of his own, leaving Pryce to learn when to step back. The Guardian describes the series as a relaxed, emotionally alert comedy rather than a conventional sports drama.

segments.title: A found family in motion
segments.body: The season’s shifts give the series room to explore loss and the mistakes Pryce cannot undo. Marc Maron, Timothy Olyphant and Rhea Seehorn add to the ensemble, while the review praises the show’s gentle humour and its thoughts on ageing, missed chances and letting younger people make their own decisions.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors finale finds a way past a chaotic series
content.shortHeadline: The Celebrity Traitors finale delivers a late surprise
content.standfirst: After a series the i Paper critic found flat and erratic, the final round brings a shock result and a win for the Faithful. The review credits contestant Bash’s lack of ego with changing the game’s last moments.

image.caption: The Endgame Round Table in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: One player’s lack of ego saved Celebrity Traitors

segments.body: The Celebrity Traitors finale ends with the Faithful winning after contestant Bash questions Kenny’s decision to end the game and persuades Romesh Ranganathan to change his vote. The i Paper review describes the outcome as a late surprise after a series in which the Faithful often missed the evidence against the Traitors.

segments.title: A change in the game
segments.body: The critic argues that Bash’s lack of ego helped him notice what others missed, while more forceful players became targets or made damaging choices. The finale also features a final mission involving a helicopter and a last round table that, in the review’s view, finally gives the series some of the tension it had lacked.

content.headline: Ocarina of Time remake review: a moving return to a landmark Zelda game
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time is a moving, ambitious remake
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake adds voiced scenes, richer detail and more accessible controls while retaining the game’s underlying story and puzzles. The Guardian review finds that its melancholy about lost childhood remains intact.

image.caption: A scene from The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true

segments.body: The Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time keeps the original’s journey through Hyrule and its puzzles, but expands dialogue and adds voiced cutscenes. The Guardian review says the changes make the story’s emotional drama clearer without changing its structure.

segments.title: The weight of time
segments.body: The remake updates movement and item selection, and gives the score a full orchestral treatment. The review praises its handmade, theatrical visual style while noting that some choices, including the loss of Sheik’s androgyny, disappoint. Its strongest response is to the story of a childhood stolen by an evil king—and to revisiting it as an adult.

content.headline: The films and TV that helped shape Grand Theft Auto
content.shortHeadline: From Heat to Boyz n the Hood: GTA’s screen influences
content.standfirst: As Grand Theft Auto 6 approaches, the Guardian traces the crime films and television that informed Rockstar’s series, from street-gang stories to the neon-lit world of Miami Vice.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto 6, a game shaped by crime films and television.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s so glossy and sexy!’: 10 movies (and one TV show) that inspired Grand Theft Auto

segments.body: Grand Theft Auto has borrowed from crime and action cinema for three decades, using films and television to shape its characters, settings and set pieces. The Guardian’s guide traces those influences from Speed and The Warriors to Scarface and Miami Vice.

segments.title: A changing crime story
segments.body: The guide links San Andreas to Boyz n the Hood and other films about Los Angeles, while describing Heat as a major reference point for GTA 5’s heists and cityscape. Across the series, it finds recurring interests in street gangs, immigration, male identity, betrayal and popular music.

content.headline: Can Alex Garland’s Elden Ring film make a story from its fantasy hellscape?
content.shortHeadline: The challenge facing Alex Garland’s Elden Ring film
content.standfirst: The adaptation has a large budget, a prominent cast and a world known for grotesque monsters and opaque lore. The Guardian argues that its biggest test is giving audiences a reason to care about that world.

image.caption: A scene from Elden Ring.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is on course to be Hollywood’s goriest ever fantasy movie

segments.body: Alex Garland’s film adaptation of Elden Ring has reportedly been shot and is in post-production, with a cast including Cailee Spaeny, Ben Whishaw and Jonathan Pryce. The Guardian essay notes the scale of the game’s audience and mythology, but warns that fantasy adaptations can fail when they explain a world without giving viewers a story to invest in.

segments.title: More than monsters
segments.body: Elden Ring’s game world leans closer to horror than familiar fantasy, with grotesque creatures and little reassurance of a happy ending. The essay considers whether Garland will draw on the history behind the Lands Between, and whether a film reportedly costing close to $200m will be allowed the bleak uncertainty that marks his earlier work.

content.headline: Playing Call of Duty with my grown-up son brought us closer
content.shortHeadline: A father and son reconnect through Call of Duty
content.standfirst: A father returns to the co-op missions he first played with his son as a child. Their improved teamwork—and the years between those attempts—turn a familiar game into a moving shared memory.

image.caption: A scene from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game a father revisits with his son.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The Guardian writer revisits Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2’s co-op missions with his 22-year-old son, nearly two decades after they first played them together. The missions they once struggled to finish become a test of how they have changed as players—and how they can still work as a team.

segments.title: A memory in the making
segments.body: They find a rhythm: the father takes aim from a distance while his son moves in close, and together they finally beat levels that once defeated them. The writer says the sessions feel carefree, and that the prospect of living in different parts of the world soon makes the time together all the more precious.

content.headline: A Zelda midnight launch brings fans together—and leaves some waiting
content.shortHeadline: Zelda fans queue overnight for a new Ocarina of Time
content.standfirst: Hundreds gathered in London for the Switch 2 remake’s midnight release, drawn by the game and collectible items. The Guardian writer finds a welcome sense of shared fandom, but a four-hour wait also tests the appeal of the old launch-day ritual.

image.caption: Fans gather for a Zelda game launch.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?

segments.body: Around 500 fans queued outside an Oxford Street shop for the midnight release of the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. The Guardian writer joined them for a limited-edition box and ocarina-shaped keyring, finding the gathering a reminder of when game launches were events to share rather than downloads to start at home.

segments.title: The wait for a keepsake
segments.body: The queue moved slowly, and after four hours some fans still had to leave their details to have the promised collectible box sent later. The writer’s affection for midnight launches survived the wait, but the night also exposed the distance between the excitement of gathering and the inconvenience of waiting in the cold.

content.headline: Stonehenge’s altar stone did not come from north-east Scotland, study finds
content.shortHeadline: Stonehenge altar stone: Scotland theory ruled out
content.standfirst: A broad geological investigation has ruled out the region proposed in 2024, but researchers say the stone’s origin remains unknown. Other possible source areas include Scotland, northern England and Ireland.

image.caption: Stonehenge’s altar stone lies beneath two sarsen stones.

sources.originalTitle: Origin of Stonehenge’s altar remains enigma as north-east Scotland theory ruled out

segments.body: Geologists tested about 70 samples from north-east Scotland against the altar stone’s composition and concluded it is very unlikely to have come from there. The research also rules out southern Britain, but does not identify where the six-tonne stone originated.

segments.title: The search continues
segments.body: The 2024 theory that the stone came from north-east Scotland had raised questions about how it was moved more than 400 miles to Stonehenge. Researchers now say other parts of Scotland, northern England or possibly Ireland remain candidates. An expert not involved in the study says finding the source would help reveal the landscape and journey known to the people who moved it.

content.headline: EU says TikTok’s recommendation system may harm users’ mental health
content.shortHeadline: EU says TikTok’s algorithm risks harmful content loops
content.standfirst: The European Commission’s preliminary findings say TikTok’s safeguards do not reliably stop repetitive feeds about themes such as body image and isolation. TikTok disputes the findings and can still respond before a final decision.

sources.originalTitle: EU charges TikTok with failing to protect users’ mental health
TikTok’s For You page needs to change, says the EU

segments.body: The European Commission says TikTok’s recommendation system can steer young and vulnerable users into repeated content about subjects such as body image, eating patterns and isolation, with a cumulative effect that may worsen anxiety or existing mental health problems. Officials say controls such as “not interested” and refreshing the feed have not proved effective.

segments.title: TikTok disputes the findings
segments.body: TikTok says the Commission’s claims misrepresent its platform and its safety work. The company says its rules prohibit content promoting disordered eating and risky weight management, and that more than 79 million EU users used its filters or “not interested” controls in the first half of 2026. The preliminary finding is part of a wider Digital Services Act investigation; TikTok can defend itself, and could face a fine of up to 6% of global turnover if the finding is upheld.

perspectives.body: TikTok’s defence is that users have direct controls over their feeds and that the company already restricts content promoting disordered eating. The Commission says those safeguards do not prevent harmful repetition.

content.headline: Cyber-attacks disrupt French blood-storage systems, but no products are lost
content.shortHeadline: Hackers disrupt French blood storage; supplies protected
content.standfirst: Hackers affected cold rooms used to store donated blood, but staff intervened before any products were lost or health impact identified. Investigators have not formally attributed the attacks.

sources.originalTitle: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits

segments.body: The French Blood Establishment said cyber-attacks affected cold rooms at medical facilities, with temperatures set to rise. Staff intervened to protect supplies; the agency reported no health impact and no loss of blood products.

segments.title: Who was behind the attacks?
segments.body: The incidents follow attacks on supermarket freezers in several European countries. Security researchers say evidence from decoy systems suggests at least one wave was targeted and coordinated, but they have not established who was responsible. Analysts have questioned claims by Russian-speaking groups, and say other actors or copycats remain possible. Authorities are investigating.

content.headline: At least 10 US communities move to restrict or drop Flock surveillance cameras
content.shortHeadline: US communities push back against Flock surveillance
content.standfirst: Local governments and police departments are ending or limiting contracts with the camera company amid concerns over privacy, data sharing and misuse. Flock says its tools help solve crimes and customers control their data.

sources.originalTitle: At least 10 local governments have moved to drop Flock’s surveillance cameras since summer

segments.body: At least 10 local governments and police departments have moved since summer to curb, restrict or end their use of Flock Safety technology. Several have cancelled contracts; residents in League City, Texas, voted against continued use of the company’s license-plate readers. Other communities have narrowed who can search the systems or how they may be used.

segments.title: Concerns over access and misuse
segments.body: Reported incidents include officers accused or convicted of using the system to track former partners. Some communities have also raised concerns about federal agencies accessing local data.
